Let the common ratio be \(r=\frac{p}{q}\) in lowest terms. Since all terms are integers, \(q^{n-1}\mid 10^{2015}\).

For the last term to be odd, its power of \(2\) must be \(0\):
\[
2015+(n-1)(v_2(p)-v_2(q))=0.
\]
Since \(p,q\) are coprime, the only way this can happen is \(v_2(p)=0\) and
\[
v_2(q)=\frac{2015}{n-1}.
\]
Thus \(n-1\mid 2015\).

Conversely, if \(d=n-1\) is any divisor of \(2015\), take
\[
r=\frac{1}{2^{2015/d}}.
\]
Then the terms are
\[
10^{2015}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{2^{2015/d}}\right)^{k-1}
=2^{2015-\frac{2015(k-1)}{d}}5^{2015},
\]
which are positive integers, and the last term is \(5^{2015}\), odd.

So the possible \(n\) correspond exactly to the positive divisors of \(2015\).

\[
2015=5\cdot 13\cdot 31
\]
has
\[
(1+1)(1+1)(1+1)=8
\]
positive divisors.

\[
\boxed{8}
\]
